did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah was commanded not to marry or have sons or daughters in the land, because the coming disaster would be so severe that the families there would not escape it.

Did you know? The chapter describes three causes of death: disease, the sword, and famine. The dead would not be buried, and their bodies would become food for the birds of the sky and the wild animals.

Did you know? Jeremiah was commanded not to enter a house of mourning or mourn with the bereaved, because the LORD said that he had taken away his peace, steadfast love, and compassion from the people.
Did you know? The destruction is also described as a complete end to social life: the sounds of joy and gladness, and the voices of bridegroom and bride, would no longer be heard.

Did you know? The people are not accused merely of repeating their ancestors’ sins; the LORD says that the present generation has done worse than its ancestors and followed the stubbornness of its evil heart.
Did you know? Alongside the prophecy of exile comes a promise of comfort: the LORD will bring the Israelites back from all the lands to the land he gave their ancestors.

Did you know? To describe the capture of the people, the chapter uses images of fishermen and hunters: first they will fish for them, and then they will hunt them from the mountains, hills, and rocky crevices.
Did you know? The chapter emphasizes that there is no way to hide one’s actions from the LORD: his eyes are on all the people’s ways, and their guilt is not hidden from him.

Did you know? Jeremiah calls the LORD his strength, fortress, and refuge in the day of trouble, and prophesies that nations will come to him and admit that the idols they inherited from their ancestors are lies and empty things that provide no help.
Did you know? The chapter ends by stating a clear purpose for the prophecy: the LORD will make his power and might known, and then everyone will know that his name is the LORD.
